deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematical derivation. It is a fair copy of part of §1, the historical introduction, of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854; published posthumously by Dedekind in 1867). The page continues the account of the 18th-century vibrating-string controversy.

(a) The left column holds only the end of footnote 4 from the previous page: 'et la propagation du son.' This completes the citation of Lagrange, 'Recherches sur la nature et la propagation du son', Misc. Taur. I (1759).

(b) Lagrange treated a massless string loaded with n equal masses at equal spacing. In modern terms this is a system of n coupled oscillators, m y_j'' = (T/a)(y_{j+1} - 2 y_j + y_{j-1}) with y_0 = y_{n+1} = 0. Its normal modes are sin(jkπ/(n+1)) with frequencies ω_k = 2 sqrt(T/(m a)) sin(kπ/(2(n+1))). Lagrange then let n tend to infinity. These formulas are my background gloss; Riemann states none of them.

(c) Riemann's judgment is as follows. The finite part was skilful, but the passage from the finite to the infinite 'left much to be desired'. As a result, d'Alembert, in the opening memoir of his Opuscules mathématiques I (1761), could keep claiming maximal generality for his own solution. The leading mathematicians stayed divided, each keeping his standpoint in later work.

(d) Riemann then summarizes the views on arbitrary functions and their trigonometric representability:
- Euler introduced arbitrary functions into analysis and applied the calculus to them on the basis of geometric intuition.
- Lagrange (Misc. Taur. II, p. 18) accepted Euler's results, i.e. the geometric construction of the motion, but was not satisfied with Euler's geometric treatment.
- D'Alembert (Opuscules I, p. 16, art. VII–XX) accepted Euler's way of handling the calculus. He contested the correctness of the results because, for wholly arbitrary functions, one cannot know whether their derivatives are continuous. The sentence continues on the next page.
errors: No mathematical errors; the page contains no computations.

Historically, the account matches the standard view and the published text of the Habilitationsschrift. Calling the decisive flaw of Lagrange's 1759 limit passage a deficiency is Riemann's (widely shared) judgment, not a demonstrable error.

results.what: Historical account of the vibrating-string controversy: Lagrange's discrete-mass model and its limit, d'Alembert's continued claim of generality, and the positions of Euler, Lagrange and d'Alembert on arbitrary functions.
results.modern_name: History of the vibrating string controversy / origins of Fourier series
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's Habilitationsschrift §1 (1854, publ. 1867) is itself the classic source for this historical survey.

results.what: D'Alembert's objection that arbitrary (Eulerian) functions may lack continuous derivatives, so the wave equation need not apply.
results.modern_name: Regularity requirement for classical solutions of the wave equation (weak vs. classical solutions)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a manuscript copy of the published historical introduction (§1) of Riemann's 1854 Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series. It is purely narrative, well known, and contains no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: Background check, not on the page: the beaded-string frequencies of Lagrange's model tend to the continuous-string frequencies k*pi*c/L as n tends to infinity (with T, rho, L, k positive). The result should be 0.
Background check: sin(j*k*pi/(n+1)) is an eigenvector of the discrete second difference with eigenvalue -4 sin^2(k*pi/(2(n+1))). The result should be 0.

transcription_corrections: The left-column line 'et la propagation du son.' is the continuation of footnote 4 from the previous page (Lagrange, Misc. Taur. Tom. I, 'Recherches sur la nature et la propagation du son'). It is not a separate heading.
In 'fortfahren konnte, seiner Lösung', the word 'seiner' is underlined in the manuscript for emphasis (d'Alembert's own solution).
The '7' in the right margin after 'Standpunkt bei.' is a marginal mark or folio number, not part of the text.

Footnote markers ¹) after 'Lagrange' and ²) after 'D'Alembert' are confirmed. The footnote reads 'Opuscules mathématiques p. d'Alembert. Tome premier. 1761. pag. 16. art. VII–XX.', consistent with the image.
